headline: High: shared filesystem, broad egress, and MCP/tooling create default risks of prompt injection, leakage, and cascading actions between Langflow and Open WebUI.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Langflow can read/write server files and chain tools in graph flows, while open-webui can ingest files, use MCP/OpenAPI tools, and run browsers. That creates a default bridge where attacker-controlled content from one can be parsed as instructions by the other, especially via shared files or tool outputs. The interaction is documented in both profiles, so uncertainty does not justify lowering severity.
conditions: IF Langflow and open-webui share any writable directory or mounted volume
IF open-webui ingests Langflow-generated files or tool outputs as prompts
IF either side forwards raw tool output into the other without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable shared writable folders between the two apps
Add a strict allowlist for file types passed between agents
Insert a provenance tag and strip instructions from transferred content
Turn off MCP/tool execution on the receiving side for untrusted inputs
requires-engineering: add sandboxing or content-disarm wrappers

B_data_leakage.rationale: Langflow touches flow inputs, intermediate outputs, and stored secrets, and open-webui touches prompts, documents, files, persistent memory, and API keys. Both have broad network egress and file access, so sensitive data can move from one agent into the other and then out to third-party APIs by default. The profiles directly support this leakage pathway.
conditions: IF both agents are deployed against the same workspace or mounted volume
IF Langflow flow inputs include secrets or regulated documents
IF open-webui is configured to send retrieved content to external model providers or search APIs
mitigations: Separate workspaces and volumes per agent
Remove secrets from shared inputs before transfer
Restrict outbound destinations to approved endpoints
Rotate any API keys exposed in shared files
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Langflow has server-side filesystem write and unsandboxed Python components, while open-webui can access local files, mounted volumes, and broad networked tools. If both are pointed at the same directory or mutable resource, concurrent writes and tool actions can overwrite each other or corrupt shared state. The profiles show overlapping write surfaces and no locking mechanism.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or mounted volume
IF Langflow Python components modify files that open-webui also edits
IF the deployment lacks external locking or per-agent namespaces
mitigations: Assign separate directories and volumes
Make shared resources read-only for one agent
Serialize writes through a single coordinator
Snapshot shared state before concurrent runs
requires-engineering: add file locks or transactional storage

D_cascading_error.rationale: Langflow is a graph-based orchestrator that can emit intermediate outputs, and open-webui supports plugins, tools, and function calling that may act on those outputs. If open-webui treats Langflow output as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into downstream actions or user-visible artifacts. Both profiles document this chain, so the risk is more than speculative.
conditions: IF open-webui consumes Langflow outputs without verification
IF Langflow is used to generate facts, code, or citations for open-webui
IF open-webui is allowed to execute tools based on those outputs
mitigations: Require human review before tool execution
Add schema validation for Langflow outputs
Cross-check critical facts against a second source
Disable auto-execution on imported outputs
requires-engineering: implement confidence gating and audit logs

E_compliance.rationale: Langflow stores per-flow credentials and processes flow inputs, while open-webui stores prompts, documents, persistent memory, and API keys. The profiles do not specify residency or certification mismatches, so a breach is not proven; however, differing retention and secret-handling surfaces create a plausible compliance gap if the same regulated data class flows through both systems.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in both agents' persistent stores
IF retention or deletion policies differ between the two deployments
IF either deployment routes regulated data to external model providers without a DPA
mitigations: Document data classes allowed in each system
Align retention and deletion settings
Keep regulated data out of persistent memory
Review vendor DPAs and residency settings
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement and audit reporting
